title: After multiple deaths and injuries, NHTSA is investigating comma.ai
content:
Aftermarket devices that can boost or augment a vehicle’s native advanced driver assistance systems are the target of a new federal investigation this week. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Office of Defects Investigation says it knows of five crashes in which drivers using devices from comma.ai crashed into stopped or slow-moving cars. Two of the crashes resulted in three deaths, and 11 people were injured in four of the five crashes, some seriously.
Comma.ai was the brainchild of George Hotz, who rose to prominence at the start of the last decade by jailbreaking iOS and hacking Sony PlayStations. In 2015, Hotz turned his attention to partially automated driver assists, which were gaining attention following Tesla’s exploits with its Autopilot system. Hotz first modified his own Acura to give it a more advanced driver assist that let him take his hands off the wheel, with the goal of selling his system to Tesla and replacing Mobileye as the company’s supplier.
(Mobileye dropped Tesla as a customer the following year after becoming unhappy with the way the car company was using Mobileye products in unintended ways.)
Comma’s first attempts to sell devices that owners could plug into their cars’ ODB port evaporated once NHTSA began asking questions in 2016. Instead, Comma decided to post its openpilot software, as well as its plans for hardware, to GitHub, allowing anyone to make the devices themselves. At first, the Comma Neo and OpenPilot supported a single Acura and single Honda model, but by 2020, the company’s software and $999 device were rated more highly by Consumer Reports than any OEM system.

report.summary: NHTSA is investigating comma.ai's aftermarket driver-assist devices after five crashes involving stopped or slow-moving vehicles, including three deaths.
report.background: The probe targets aftermarket advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS), which can augment a car's native safety features. Comma.ai was founded by George Hotz, known for jailbreaking iOS and hacking Sony PlayStation. In 2015, Hotz modified an Acura to provide hands-off driver assist, aiming to sell the system to Tesla and replace Mobileye as its supplier. Mobileye later dropped Tesla over unintended product use. When NHTSA asked questions in 2016, Comma.ai abandoned plans to sell plug-in OBD devices and instead published openpilot software and hardware plans on GitHub. The open-source approach let enthusiasts build their own systems. By 2020, Consumer Reports rated comma.ai's software and $999 device higher than any OEM driver-assist system, showing both the potential and the regulatory gray zone for aftermarket automation.
key_points: Federal safety probe: NHTSA's Office of Defects Investigation knows of five crashes where drivers using comma.ai devices hit stopped or slow-moving cars. Two crashes caused three deaths, and four of the five crashes injured 11 people, some seriously. This is a major test for aftermarket driver-assist oversight.

Origin story: George Hotz founded comma.ai after gaining fame for jailbreaking iOS and hacking Sony consoles. In 2015 he modified his own Acura for hands-off driving, hoping to sell the technology to Tesla and displace Mobileye. Tesla's Autopilot had already made partial automation a high-profile industry target.

Open-source pivot: After NHTSA inquiries in 2016, comma.ai canceled plans to sell plug-and-play OBD devices. It posted openpilot software and hardware designs on GitHub, letting users assemble their own systems. Early versions supported only one Acura and one Honda model.

Mainstream validation: By 2020, Consumer Reports rated comma.ai's openpilot software and $999 device above every OEM driver-assist system it tested. That success demonstrated open-source ADAS could outperform factory systems, but it also spread advanced automation beyond traditional automaker and dealer oversight.

Safety and liability questions: The crashes raise concerns about whether aftermarket systems can reliably detect stopped traffic, and who is responsible when open-source driver assist fails. Regulators may push for recalls, software limits, driver monitoring, or clearer warnings that these are not self-driving systems.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the investigation could slow aftermarket autonomy and push regulators to treat driver-assist software more like safety-critical vehicle components, requiring certification and reporting. Developers of open-source ADAS may face pressure to add driver monitoring, operational limits, and formal safety cases. Automakers could distance themselves from third-party modifications, while investors grow cautious about consumer autonomy startups. For regular users, comma.ai devices may still offer convenience, but the probe reinforces that no current system is fully self-driving. Owners must supervise the road, and crashes can trigger recalls or restrictions that affect thousands of vehicles. The outcome may set precedent for how federal regulators oversee software-defined vehicle features.
report.tools: Follow NHTSA's ODI investigation docket for official findings. For technical context, review comma.ai's openpilot on GitHub, its comma three hardware, and community forks like sunnypilot and FrogPilot. Broader open-source ADAS projects include Autoware and Apollo, while CARLA and LGSVL simulators help test automated-driving safety scenarios.
